description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de tercer semestre de Ingeniería en Tecnologías Computacionales en la UDEM. Nos gusta usar la tecnología y los datos abiertos de la NASA para crear soluciones innovadoras a retos reales, combinando programación, diseño y trabajo en equipo.
summary:
QUEST(ION) is a browser-based pixel-art educational game where the player designs a Mars mission from start to finish, inspired by NASA’s Spirit and Opportunity rovers. Players choose spacecraft systems, pack science instruments, plan an Earth–Mars trajectory using real JPL Horizons data, hunt for rocks with evidence of ancient water, and decide how to send data back to Earth. Eight mini-games turn each decision into hands-on action. A final dashboard then compares every choice with what the real NASA team did (MATCH / CLOSE / DIFFERENT).

It addresses the challenge by showing the decision-making behind space exploration, with its trade-offs in budget, mass, energy and fuel, instead of only the finished results. It matters because it teaches scientific thinking (questions, evidence, trade-offs) using verifiable NASA/JPL sources. Invented gameplay numbers are clearly labeled as simulated, and narration and accessibility options let anyone learn without prior knowledge.
details:
What it does and how it works.

The game is a linear six-stage journey: plan the mission, build the spacecraft, travel, explore, communicate, and review. In the Workshop, the player installs 5 spacecraft systems, and option B is always the real MER configuration. In the Warehouse, the player picks from 14 instruments. In Orbit, the player picks a launch date, travel time and a fuel-vs-speed criterion, and the game computes delta-v from real Earth and Mars positions. In Rock Hunter, the player scans rocks, and what each scan reveals depends on the instruments packed earlier. The Comms Planner and Signal Run cover sending data home, including light-time delay and orbiter passes. Decisions carry forward, and live meters track budget, mass and energy.

Benefits.

  • Players get immediate feedback, and quizzes explain mistakes without punishing them.
  • Every decision is compared with the real mission.
  • A personalized learning review gives extra practice on the concepts the player missed, in five formats (Visual, Podcast, Flashcards, Questions, Text).
  • Accessibility features include a narrator that reads the screen, three text sizes, volume control and reduced motion.

Intended impact.

Players should finish the videogame understanding that a mission starts with a scientific question, that every engineering choice has a cost, that evidence of water comes from analyzing rocks and not from a photo, and that data from Mars arrives late and through limited windows.

Tools and technology.

  • Phaser 3 and JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), published on GitHub Pages
  • A Node.js server (server.mjs) for the narrator endpoint and a JPL Horizons proxy
  • NASA/JPL Horizons API, with a Lambert solver for the transfer trajectories
  • Gemini text-to-speech for the narrator
  • Figma for design and art
  • Hand-written (no libraries) data structures (Stack, Queue, LinkedList, MinHeap, Graph, sorting) with automated tests
  • Press Start 2P and VT323 fonts (SIL OFL) and Pixabay music
  • Claude Code for development assistance

Creativity.

Instead of a quiz about space, the player plays the mission designer. Earlier choices change later outcomes, because the instruments you pack determine what you can read in Rock Hunter. The “real vs. simulated” labeling is built into the interface. The Earth–Mars trajectory uses real ephemeris data, and the game begins by asking the player to draw the path they expect before showing the computed one.


Factors considered.

  • Every educational fact comes from an official NASA/JPL page and carries a source URL, and gameplay numbers are marked SIMULATED GAME VALUE.
  • No NASA logos or insignia appear anywhere.
  • Accessibility.
  • The game works as a static site when the server is unavailable.
  • Players are never stuck: failed quizzes show an easier question, and mini-games can be retried.
